days.title: Prompts, Model Tasks and Chain Components

concepts.heading: Shaping the Output Format with Roles, Examples and Sampling
concepts.body: A chat request is a list of messages with roles: system, user and assistant. Put standing rules such as language, tone, length and what to do when the context lacks the answer in the system message, and send only the changing question and retrieved passages in the user message. This role layout is the common chat API convention (generic, not a Databricks feature), and every request must carry all the messages the model should see. Three generic levers then steer the format. Few-shot examples show two or three inputs, each followed by exactly the output the application expects, and models copy a shown pattern more reliably than a described one. Asking for step-by-step work followed by a final line with a fixed marker such as Total: helps multi-rule problems, because the result is computed in steps and code can read the last line. Sampling matters too: in Foundation Model APIs temperature is a number from 0 to 2, where 0 is deterministic and higher values add randomness, so label and extraction tasks should use a low value.

concepts.heading: Constrained Output with response_format
concepts.body: When a program must parse the reply, do not rely on wording alone. Foundation Model APIs chat endpoints accept a response_format field with three types: text, json_object and json_schema. Use json_schema when the shape is fixed and known: the model follows the schema you supply. Use json_object when the fields are not known at development time: the model returns a valid JSON object, you name the wanted fields in the prompt, and your code must check that the keys are present because only the syntax is guaranteed. Claude models accept only json_schema, and for free output you simply omit response_format. Foundation Model APIs support just a subset of JSON schema. Regular expressions with pattern, anyOf, oneOf, allOf, prefixItems and $ref are not supported, and a list of types works only as [type, "null"]. A flat schema also generates better JSON, so move such rules into field descriptions and validate in code. If the JSON stops in the middle of a string, a token ceiling such as max_tokens most likely cut the reply, so raise it (generic troubleshooting). In SQL, ai_query takes a responseFormat argument for the same purpose.

concepts.heading: Matching the Model Task to the Business Need
concepts.body: Decide the task first, then the tool. Generation models write text: answers, rewrites and summaries. Embedding models map text to vectors so that similar meaning lands close together; they serve semantic search, clustering and the retrieval step of RAG, and they never write text. Classification assigns labels, and parsing turns files into text, tables and layout. In SQL these jobs are AI Functions. The task-specific functions each do one job: ai_parse_document reads PDF, image, Word and PowerPoint files held in a binary column, ai_extract pulls the fields of a schema you define, ai_classify assigns labels you provide, and ai_translate, ai_summarize and ai_mask do what their names say. Databricks recommends them for getting started because they need no customization. ai_query is the general-purpose function: you write the prompt and choose a supported model, which gives the most flexibility and the most design work. For private knowledge that changes weekly, retrieval plus generation fits better than tuning, because passages are read at question time while tuned weights stay a snapshot (a generic argument).

concepts.heading: Chain Components and Their Order
concepts.body: A chain is a sequence of components in which each accepts the output type of the one before. In a RAG chain the user question enters as a string. The retriever turns it into documents (on Databricks an AI Search index), a formatting step joins them into one context string, the prompt template fills its named variables such as context and question, the chat model (ChatDatabricks in the databricks-langchain package) returns a message object, and an output parser such as StrOutputParser converts that message into a plain string. LangChain Expression Language writes this with the pipe operator; the pattern is generic LangChain, not a Databricks feature. Two failures recur. A template that declares context and question fails before the model is called when the chain input has other keys, so a first dict step must map the retriever output to context and pass the question through. And code that expects a string needs the parser, because a model returns a message. To cite sources, the retrieval step must return source columns such as title and URL, and the prompt must show them beside each passage.

examPoints: Use response_format for machine-readable output: json_schema for a known shape (flat, no pattern, anyOf or $ref), json_object when the fields are unknown; JSON cut off mid-string means max_tokens is too low.

Pick the task first: embeddings for semantic similarity, chat models for generation, ai_parse_document for files, ai_classify and ai_extract for labels and fields; ai_query is the flexible general-purpose function.
A RAG chain runs retriever, prompt template, chat model, output parser; the template variables must match the dict that enters it, and sources survive only if retrieval returns them.

quiz.q: An extraction service sends a json_schema response format to a Foundation Model APIs chat endpoint. The schema gives currency a regular expression pattern and price an anyOf of string and number, and the request fails. The service still needs schema-shaped output. What should the team do?
choices: Switch to json_object, which applies the regular expression from the schema while the reply is decoded
Move the anyOf branches into a $ref definition so that the endpoint resolves the alternatives by reference
Use flat string and number properties, describe the currency rule in the field, and validate in code
Raise the temperature to 2 so that the model explores formats that happen to satisfy the pattern
quiz.explain: Foundation Model APIs support only a subset of JSON schema, and pattern, anyOf and $ref are outside it. A flat typed schema stays inside the subset, and the rule that cannot be expressed moves to the field description and an application-side check. json_object guarantees valid JSON but applies no schema, and temperature only changes randomness.

quiz.q: Analysts must label each of three million rows of a Unity Catalog table with one of six topic labels using SQL. They have no prompt-writing experience and want the least setup. Which option fits best?
choices: ai_classify with the six topic labels passed as its labels argument
ai_query with a hand-written prompt for each row and a custom parser that cleans every free-text reply
ai_parse_document applied to the text column so that each row is split into topics automatically
An embedding model whose vectors are stored in the table and read back as the label for every row
quiz.explain: ai_classify is the task-specific function built for assigning labels you provide, and Databricks recommends task-specific functions for getting started because they need no customization. ai_query works but brings the prompt and parsing work the team wants to avoid. ai_parse_document reads files, and embeddings are vectors, not labels.

days.recap: Control format with roles, examples, low temperature and response_format (json_schema for known shapes, json_object for unknown fields, within the supported schema subset). Choose embeddings, generation, parsing, classification or extraction by task, using task-specific AI Functions before ai_query, and order chain components so each output type fits the next input.

days.title: Business Goals, Tools and Current Agent Building Blocks

concepts.heading: Turning a Business Goal into Pipeline Inputs and Outputs
concepts.body: A goal such as cutting the time reps spend searching old RFP answers is not yet a design. Restate it as what goes in and what comes out, then ask a few generic design questions. Who waits? An interactive chat user needs the first words quickly, so the output is a streamed response (the Chat Completions stream parameter sends server-sent events), while table-wide work that nobody watches is a scheduled batch job applying an AI Function to a column. What does the consumer need? A person reads cited prose with a not-found statement; a reporting table needs a typed record per item, with a rule for missing values such as null. Which user attributes change the result? If agents may see only articles for their own region, the region is an input and retrieval filters on it, because AI Search queries accept filters on metadata columns. Writing the goal this way fixes the components before any code: retrieval or not, one model call or several, and what the final answer looks like.

concepts.heading: Defining and Ordering Tools for Multi-Stage Reasoning
concepts.body: An agent runs a loop: it reasons with a model, calls tools to gather information or change the state of another system, observes the results and repeats until it can answer. With function calling the model does not run anything. You describe each function with a description and a JSON schema for its parameters, and the model returns a JSON object with the arguments; your code runs the function and appends the result as a new message. The tool_choice setting defaults to auto, can require some tool, force one named function, or be none. Order tools by data dependency, a generic rule: the tool that produces an input (an order lookup returning a product category) runs before the one that consumes it (a policy search for that category). Pick the tool by data type: exact figures from a governed table suit a parameterized SQL function in Unity Catalog, unstructured text suits an AI Search index. A Unity Catalog function tool needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and EXECUTE for the caller, and the Function Client runs it on serverless compute.

concepts.heading: Current Agent Building Blocks on Databricks
concepts.body: Agent Bricks covers the workflows for building a production agent in code. Agent Runtime hosts agents built with any framework or harness, stateful or stateless, and AgentKit adds durable execution so that runs survive restarts and crashes. Databricks Sandbox gives an agent an isolated place to run the code it writes, and MLflow Tracing records each step. The Agent Bricks CLI scaffolds a project, runs it locally and deploys it. Unity Gateway gives one API for models and also governs MCP servers and skills with guardrails, rate limits and usage tracking. For low-code work, Genie Agents are domain environments where the data team configures trusted data, metrics and business rules, and a custom agent can call a Genie Agent as a tool. Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent are marked Legacy, and the docs point to Genie Agents for new low-code agents and the Agent Bricks CLI for new agents in code. The exam guide still uses the older names, so recognise them but do not key them as the recommended design.

concepts.heading: AI Functions for Batch Document Work
concepts.body: Not every GenAI need is an agent. Suppose forty thousand supplier contracts sit as PDFs in a Unity Catalog volume and a scheduled job must write vendor, term and renewal date to a table. Nobody chats, so the right shape is batch extraction in SQL. Read the files with the binaryFile format so that each document is a binary column, apply ai_parse_document to get structured elements (text, tables, layout), then pass that output to ai_extract with a schema naming the three fields. ai_extract accepts the output of ai_parse_document directly, which makes the two-step flow composable, and the documents are processed inside the Databricks security perimeter. For labelling rows you would use ai_classify with the labels you provide, and for a fully custom prompt ai_query. Databricks suggests Databricks-hosted foundation models (names starting with databricks-) rather than provisioned throughput for ai_query batch work. Put the statements in a job or Lakeflow pipeline for scheduled runs. An index and a chat agent would add cost and moving parts without improving this table-filling task.

examPoints: Write a goal as pipeline input and output: interactive users get streamed text, table-wide work becomes a scheduled batch job, tables need typed records with a null rule, and a per-user attribute becomes an input that filters retrieval.

The model only proposes a tool call as JSON; application code runs it and returns the result. Order tools by data dependency; Unity Catalog function tools need EXECUTE (plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA) and serverless compute for the Function Client.
New agents: code on Agent Bricks (CLI, Agent Runtime, AgentKit), low-code on Genie Agents, table filling with ai_parse_document plus ai_extract. Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent are Legacy.

quiz.q: A team runs an agent built with its own Python framework. Long research runs sometimes die when the host restarts, and the team wants managed hosting without rewriting the agent. Which capability fits?
choices: A Knowledge Assistant, which replaces the custom framework with a managed question-and-answer chatbot over documents
A Genie Agent configured over the tables that the research uses, so that the agent no longer needs code
A scheduled job that calls ai_query once per research step and stores each reply in a Delta table
Agent Runtime with AgentKit, which hosts any framework and adds durable execution
quiz.explain: Agent Runtime hosts agents built with any framework or harness, and AgentKit adds durable execution so that runs survive restarts and crashes. Knowledge Assistant is Legacy and replaces the agent rather than hosting it, a Genie Agent is a low-code product for data questions, and a job of single ai_query calls gives no durable agent loop.

quiz.q: An agent tool is a SQL-backed Unity Catalog function. The notebook is attached only to a SQL warehouse, no serverless compute is enabled in the workspace, and the Function Client cannot run the tool. What does the documentation require?
choices: A larger SQL warehouse, since the Function Client sends the tool query to the warehouse that the notebook uses
Serverless compute, since the Function Client runs tools on serverless general compute
Ownership of the catalog, since a caller can run the tool only when it owns the function's parent catalog
A provisioned throughput endpoint for the model, since tool calls are billed only on dedicated serving compute
quiz.explain: The Function Client runs Unity Catalog function tools on serverless general compute, and a SQL warehouse alone is not sufficient. Calling a function needs EXECUTE on it with USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents, not ownership, and the model endpoint type is unrelated to where the tool runs.

days.recap: Translate a goal into inputs and outputs by asking who waits, what the consumer needs and which user attribute filters retrieval. Tools are described to the model, which only proposes calls; order them by data dependency and use governed Unity Catalog functions for exact figures. Build new agents with Agent Bricks in code or Genie Agents without code, and use AI Functions for batch document work.

days.title: Chunking, Cleaning and Parsing Source Documents

concepts.heading: Chunking for Document Structure and Model Limits
concepts.body: Chunking breaks parsed data into semantically concentrated pieces so that retrieved text fits the model's context and carries little distracting material. The Databricks RAG pipeline guidance names four families. Fixed-size chunking splits by a preset count of characters or tokens, is quick to set up and rarely gives coherent chunks, so the guidance says it rarely works for production applications. Paragraph-based chunking follows natural boundaries (the LangChain RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter is the example). Format-specific chunking uses the structure of Markdown or HTML, such as headers. Semantic chunking finds topic shifts, for example with the LangChain SemanticChunker. There is no one-size-fits-all choice, so the work is iterative and driven by the data. Chunk size is a trade-off: small chunks focus on details and lose surrounding context, large chunks keep context and add irrelevant text. The embedding model also sets a ceiling. Text beyond its maximum token limit is truncated, which silently drops information, so size chunks below that limit.

concepts.heading: Overlap, Tables and Metadata
concepts.body: Three refinements follow from the same goal of self-contained chunks. Overlap repeats a small slice of text at the edge of neighbouring chunks, which the docs say preserves continuity so that a fact next to a boundary is not separated from its context. Keep it modest, because heavy overlap fills the index with near-copies. Tables need their own handling (generic practice): treat each table as a unit apart from prose, split only between rows, and repeat the header row in every piece, so that a retrieved fragment still shows which column a value belongs to. Metadata completes the chunk. The pipeline guidance lists document-level fields (file name, URL, version, timestamps), structural fields (section headers, page numbers) and content fields (keywords, summaries). Stored beside the chunk text, they let retrieval filter and let the application cite a source, so write source path, section title and page as extra columns instead of leaving only a chunk id and text. Semantic coherence still matters most.

concepts.heading: Filtering Content That Degrades Retrieval
concepts.body: Clean the corpus before chunking, because every repeated or wrong chunk competes with useful ones. Remove running headers, footers and page numbers; the ai_parse_document output tags elements with types such as page_header, page_footer and page_number, so they can be dropped by type. Each element also carries a confidence from 0 to 1, and a threshold, chosen by reviewing a sample of the parsed output, can remove garbled text from poor scans (the threshold is generic practice; the docs advise evaluating parsing quality on samples). Deduplicate next: exact copies can be caught with metadata such as title and creation date, and near-copies with MinHash, a locality-sensitive hashing technique available in Spark ML. The recipe is to build feature vectors, fit a MinHash model for Jaccard distance, run a similarity join and filter the duplicates, keeping the best version, for example the most recently updated or most authoritative. Finally filter out documents that are irrelevant, too old, unreliable or harmful, using metadata such as status and effective date, a toxicity classifier or PII detection.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Package That Extracts the Content
concepts.body: The parser follows the source format. For text documents such as PDF and Word files, the pipeline guidance names off-the-shelf libraries such as unstructured and PyPDF2. For HTML pages, use an HTML parser such as BeautifulSoup or lxml to select the elements you want. Images and scanned documents have no text layer, so optical character recognition is required, with open source engines such as Tesseract or services such as Amazon Textract, Azure AI Vision OCR and Google Cloud Vision. Inside Databricks the AI Function ai_parse_document covers layout-aware parsing from SQL. It reads PDF, JPG, PNG, TIFF, DOC, DOCX, PPT and PPTX content stored as a binary column, which you can create from a Unity Catalog volume with the binaryFile reader, and it returns elements such as text, tables (as HTML), figures, headers and footers. Document data stays inside the Databricks security perimeter. Whatever parser you use, log errors, since failures often point to upstream source problems, and look at a sample of the output regularly.

examPoints: Fixed-size splitting ignores meaning; prefer paragraph (recursive) or format-specific splitting, keep chunks below the embedding model's maximum tokens, add modest overlap, and store source, section and page as metadata columns.

Before chunking: drop headers, footers and page numbers, deduplicate (metadata for exact copies, MinHash for near copies, keep the best version), and filter old, irrelevant, harmful or sensitive documents using metadata such as status and effective date.
Parser by format: unstructured or PyPDF2 for text documents, BeautifulSoup or lxml for HTML, OCR for images and scans, and ai_parse_document for layout-aware parsing from SQL over a binary column.

quiz.q: Parsed router manuals still carry the running header "Acme Router Guide - Confidential", a footer and a page number on every page. Retrieval for many different questions returns chunks dominated by that repeated text. Parsing used ai_parse_document. What should the engineer do before chunking?
choices: Keep every element and raise the chunk overlap, since repeated text matters only when chunks are too short
Drop the elements typed page_header, page_footer and page_number from the parsed output
Embed the repeated text once and attach its vector to every chunk of the same manual in the index
Replace the embedding model with a larger one that learns by itself to ignore the repeated lines
quiz.explain: Parsed output labels layout elements by type, so the noise can be removed by dropping those types before chunking. More overlap would copy the repeated text into even more chunks, and a different embedding model still embeds the noise it is given.

quiz.q: A contract-search RAG index was built with a fixed-size splitter that cuts every document into pieces of equal length. Retrieved chunks often begin in the middle of a sentence and end mid-clause, so answers quote half a clause. What is the best change to the chunking step?
choices: Shrink the pieces until each holds a single word so that no clause can be cut at an unlucky place
Enlarge the pieces to the whole document so that a clause can never be cut by a boundary
Keep the splitter and add a second embedding model that repairs sentences at retrieval time
Use a recursive splitter that tries paragraph and sentence boundaries before cutting by length
quiz.explain: Boundaries that follow paragraphs and sentences keep clauses together, which is what paragraph-based splitters such as the recursive splitter do. Single-word pieces destroy meaning, whole-document pieces add noise and may exceed the embedding model's limit, and an embedding model cannot repair already broken text.

days.recap: Chunk along paragraphs, headers or topics rather than blind lengths, within the embedding model's limit, with modest overlap and metadata columns. Clean first: remove layout noise, duplicates and unreliable documents. Choose the parser by format, and use ai_parse_document for layout-aware parsing from SQL.

days.title: Delta Chunk Tables, Source Selection and Retrieval Metrics

concepts.heading: Writing Chunks to Delta in Unity Catalog
concepts.body: The Databricks pipeline guidance says to keep raw source data in a target table, which preserves it for traceability and auditing, and to ingest it incrementally. A typical sequence (assembled from the guidance's components, generic) is: land the raw files, parse them, chunk the text, give every chunk a unique id, write the chunks and their metadata to a Delta table in Unity Catalog, and create the AI Search index on that table. Chunks and metadata sit in the same Delta table that backs the index, which lets queries filter on metadata. A Delta Sync index keeps itself in step with that source table. On a standard endpoint the source table must use a change data feed, set with the table property delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true, and a table with row tracking enabled gets a change data feed automatically. The column name _id is reserved, so rename such a source column. A Direct Access index is different: you update it yourself through the REST API. To keep nightly runs cheap, re-chunk only the documents that changed and apply them with MERGE (a generic Delta pattern), so the change feed stays small.

concepts.heading: Choosing Source Documents for a RAG Application
concepts.body: A RAG application cannot retrieve what is not in its corpus, and the docs advise spending time on the nuances of the data and involving domain experts and stakeholders from the start. They help list the questions users will really ask and rank the content that matters most, such as knowledge-base articles, FAQs, manuals and troubleshooting guides for a support bot. Check coverage by mapping each realistic question to a document that answers it (a generic test). Then judge quality. Prefer sources that are current, owned by someone who can confirm them, and versioned, and store version and effective date as metadata, so that a legal PDF with a version number beats an anonymous wiki page edited four years ago. Volume and file format are not the test. Provenance matters as well. The guidance advises keeping raw source data for traceability and lists file name, URL and timestamps as document-level metadata; keeping the source path and timestamps is therefore a sensible way (generic practice) to trace a quoted passage back to the file version it came from.

concepts.heading: Retrieval Metrics
concepts.body: Retrieval is evaluated against a labeled set that lists, for each question, which documents are relevant. The metrics below are generic information-retrieval definitions, not Databricks features. Precision@k is the number of relevant results in the top k divided by k. Recall@k is the number of relevant results in the top k divided by all relevant documents that exist. If a retriever returns five chunks, two are relevant, and four relevant chunks exist in the index, precision@5 is 2/5 = 0.4 and recall@5 is 2/4 = 0.5. Both ignore order inside the cut-off, so a rank-aware metric is needed when the model reads only the first few chunks. Mean reciprocal rank averages 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result: first hits at ranks 1, 2 and 4 give (1 + 0.5 + 0.25) / 3, about 0.58. NDCG rewards placing highly relevant items near the top using graded labels. Without labeled relevant document identifiers per question, recall cannot be computed at all.

concepts.heading: Measuring Retrieval with MLflow on Databricks
concepts.body: MLflow can only judge a retriever it recognises. The documented standard is a retriever function that returns a list of Document objects, with attributes such as doc_uri and similarity_score in the metadata field, and that is traced with the RETRIEVER span type (mlflow.trace(span_type="RETRIEVER")). The doc_uri is the primary identifier of a returned document: the review app shows it so reviewers can trace the origin of an answer, and it is the identifier used to compare retriever results with ground-truth evaluation sets. The older route of calling mlflow.models.set_retriever_schema to map custom column names is documented as legacy and deprecated, so new retrievers should return Document objects instead. Built-in judges cover the retrieval step too. RetrievalRelevance asks whether the retrieved context is relevant to the request and needs no ground truth, while RetrievalSufficiency asks whether the context holds all facts needed for the expected answer and therefore needs expectations. RetrievalGroundedness checks that the response is grounded in the context.

examPoints: Chunk pipeline order: land raw files, parse, chunk, give each chunk a unique key, write a Unity Catalog Delta table with change data feed (row tracking also works), then create the Delta Sync index; _id is reserved, and MERGE only changed documents.

Choose sources that answer real questions and are current, owned and versioned; keep raw files with source path and timestamps for traceability, and verify coverage with domain experts and real questions.

Precision@k = relevant in top k / k; recall@k = relevant in top k / all relevant; MRR and NDCG are rank-aware (generic). MLflow retrievers return Document objects with doc_uri in a RETRIEVER span; set_retriever_schema is deprecated.

quiz.q: A job writes chunks to a new managed Delta table with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT. Creating a Delta Sync index on a standard AI Search endpoint over that table fails with an error about the source table's change tracking. What is the fix?
choices: Enable change data feed on the table, then create the index
Rename the unique key column to _id, which is the name the index reserves for row keys
Copy the chunk table into a Unity Catalog volume as JSON files and point the index at the volume path
Create the index first and let its first sync switch on change tracking for the source table afterwards
quiz.explain: On a standard endpoint a Delta Sync index needs a change data feed on its source table (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true), or row tracking, which provides one automatically. The name _id is reserved and must be avoided in the source table, an index is built on a table rather than loose files, and the sync does not turn on change tracking by itself.

quiz.q: A retriever returns five chunks for an evaluation question and two of them are relevant. The labeled evaluation set says that four chunks in the whole index are relevant to this question. What are precision@5 and recall@5?
choices: Precision@5 is 0.5 and recall@5 is 0.4, because precision divides by all relevant chunks that exist
Precision@5 is 0.8 and recall@5 is 0.5, because precision divides the four relevant chunks by five
Precision@5 is 0.4 and recall@5 is 0.5
Precision@5 is 0.4 and recall@5 is 1.0, because recall divides the two hits by the two chunks found
quiz.explain: Precision@5 is the two relevant results among five returned, 2/5 = 0.4. Recall@5 is the two relevant results found among the four that exist in the index, 2/4 = 0.5. The other values swap the denominators or divide by the wrong set.

days.recap: Write chunks with metadata and a unique key to a Unity Catalog Delta table with change data feed, then build the Delta Sync index, updating only changed documents. Choose current, owned, versioned sources and keep raw files for traceability. Evaluate retrieval with precision, recall, MRR and NDCG against labeled relevant documents, and give MLflow Document objects with doc_uri in RETRIEVER spans.

days.title: Advanced Chunking Designs and Re-ranking

concepts.heading: The Trade-off That Advanced Chunking Resolves
concepts.body: Day 3 left an open tension. The Databricks pipeline guidance says smaller chunks focus on specific details but lose surrounding context, while larger chunks capture context but include irrelevant information and cost more to process. There is no single best size, so the choice is iterative. The advanced designs avoid choosing: they use one chunk shape for matching and another for what the model reads. A typical symptom is an insurance assistant whose small chunks match the question precisely but leave out the surrounding clauses, while large chunks give complete context and make retrieval noisy. The designs in this day are generic retrieval patterns that you build in your own pipeline from Delta tables and an AI Search index. They are not named Databricks features, and the exam asks you to pick the right pattern for a symptom. Start by naming the symptom: boundary loss, missing subject, missing neighbours or noisy large chunks.

concepts.heading: Parent-Child and Sentence-Window Retrieval
concepts.body: Parent-child retrieval separates matching from reading. Split a document into large parent sections, then split each parent into small child chunks and store the parent identifier in a column on every child. Embed and search the children for precision, then use the parent id of each hit to fetch the larger parent section, which goes into the prompt. In a Databricks pipeline the children live in the Delta table behind the index and the parents in another Delta table or column. Several hits can share a parent, so de-duplicate parents before building the prompt. Sentence-window retrieval is the same idea at a finer grain: embed single sentences and store their position, then return each hit together with a fixed number of sentences on each side. It suits answers that depend on one sentence whose neighbours explain an exception. Both designs improve context at generation time without making the embedded unit larger, and both cost extra storage and a lookup step (generic patterns).

concepts.heading: Adding Context to Chunks and Semantic Chunking
concepts.body: Chunks such as "It must be replaced every year" fail because the subject is missing, so queries that name the product never match them. Two generic fixes add the context. Prepend the document title and section heading to the chunk text before embedding, so that the vector carries the subject. And store the heading path and a short document summary as metadata columns beside the chunk, so that they are returned with it and can be read by a reranker. Semantic chunking is another advanced option. It places boundaries where the topic changes, for example by comparing embeddings of adjacent sentences, and the Databricks guidance cites topic-shift approaches such as the LangChain SemanticChunker. The result is coherent chunks of variable size, but the method needs embedding calls at ingestion time, which matters when millions of pages are re-chunked after each policy change (a generic cost argument). Recursive splitting is cheaper and predictable. Choose by the evaluation results of both.

concepts.heading: Re-ranking in AI Search
concepts.body: Re-ranking is a second stage. The first stage retrieves a candidate set quickly, and the AI Search reranker then re-evaluates each retrieved document for semantic relevance to the query. Databricks calls it a research-based compound AI system (rerankers in general are often cross-encoders that read query and passage together, a generic description), and recommends trying it for any RAG agent use case. The price is a small latency delay, so, as a generic judgement, it suits quality-first applications such as RAG chatbots more than latency-critical lookups such as autocomplete. In the Python SDK you pass reranker=DatabricksReranker(columns_to_rerank=["text", "parent_doc_summary"]) from databricks.ai_search.reranker. The columns to return (columns) and the metadata columns the reranker may read (columns_to_rerank) are set separately. The order of columns_to_rerank matters because the calculation considers only the leading part of the text. num_results is the final number of results returned and does not change how many results are reranked. If the reranker call fails, results come back unreranked with a warning.

examPoints: Small chunks match precisely but lack context, large chunks give context but retrieve noisily: parent-child (search children, return the parent) and sentence-window (embed sentences, return neighbours) resolve it. They are generic patterns built in your pipeline.

Context-poor chunks: prepend title and section heading to the embedded text and store heading path and summary as metadata. Semantic chunking gives coherent variable-size chunks at a higher ingestion cost; recursive splitting is cheap and predictable.

A reranker is an optional second stage that re-scores retrieved candidates against the query: it trades a little latency for relevance. columns_to_rerank is separate from columns and ordered; num_results is the final count.

quiz.q: A RAG assistant answers questions about long insurance policies. Chunks of about 150 tokens match the question precisely but leave out the surrounding clauses, and chunks of about 1,500 tokens give full context but make retrieval noisy. Which design addresses both problems?
choices: Split the documents into non-overlapping chunks of about 800 tokens, a size that is a compromise between the two
Embed the 1,500-token sections and ask the model to decide which sentences matter after retrieval
Embed small child chunks carrying a parent identifier, then pass the larger parent section to the model
Keep the 150-token chunks and raise the number of results returned until all clauses of the policy appear
quiz.explain: Parent-child retrieval searches small chunks for precision and returns their larger parent for context, so one design serves both goals. A single mid-sized chunk keeps both weaknesses in part, noisy embeddings of large sections remain, and returning many small hits does not restore the clauses around them in order.

quiz.q: A developer adds the AI Search reranker to a query with columns_to_rerank set to product_name and parent_doc_summary, and num_results set to 5. Which statement is correct?
choices: num_results is the final result count and does not change how many candidates are reranked
columns_to_rerank replaces the columns list, so the returned rows contain only the two reranking columns
The order of the names in columns_to_rerank is ignored because every listed column is scored on its own
The reranker must be switched on for the whole endpoint beforehand and cannot be passed with an individual query
quiz.explain: The columns to return and the columns for reranking are set separately, num_results is the final count, and it does not affect how many results the reranker scores. The order of columns_to_rerank matters, and the reranker is requested per query in the SDK call.

days.recap: Advanced chunking decouples what is matched from what is read: parent-child and sentence-window retrieval, plus headings and summaries added to context-poor chunks. Semantic chunking buys coherence at ingestion cost. A reranker re-scores a candidate set for better relevance at the price of latency, so use it for quality-first RAG and skip it for latency-critical lookups.

days.title: LangChain Tooling, Qualitative Review and Chunking Chosen by Evidence

concepts.heading: Choosing LangChain and the Databricks integrations
concepts.body: LangChain and LangGraph are open-source frameworks for composing several steps: retrieval, prompt templates, tool calls, branching and state. Databricks supplies its integrations in the `databricks-langchain` package, imported as `databricks_langchain`. `ChatDatabricks(endpoint=...)` wraps a Model Serving endpoint, including a Foundation Model API endpoint, as a LangChain chat model. `VectorSearchRetrieverTool` exposes a Databricks AI Search index (formerly Vector Search) as an agent tool; Databricks recommends this AI Bridge tool for new Python agents, and its tool description is the text the LLM reads when it decides whether to search. `UCFunctionToolkit` turns Unity Catalog functions into tools, and its `.tools` list goes to the agent. The function client runs in serverless mode by default, which handles SQL and Python functions. `execution_mode="local"` runs trusted Python functions in a local subprocess for testing and does not support SQL functions. Generic rule, not a Databricks one: choose the lightest tool. One prompt applied to every row of a table needs no chain, so call the model directly, for example with `ai_query` over the table.

concepts.heading: Qualitative assessment: label the failure first
concepts.body: Qualitative assessment means reading real inputs, retrieved context and outputs, then naming the failure before choosing a fix. In an MLflow trace the retriever span shows what came back and the LLM span shows what was generated from it. If the retrieved passages are off-topic, even a faithful model writes a fluent wrong answer, so repair retrieval: chunking, embeddings, filters. If the passages are right but the answer adds claims they do not support, the fault is in generation, so tighten the prompt or the model settings. Replies that all stop mid-sentence at about the same length point to an output token limit, so check the `max_tokens` setting and the `finish_reason` in the response (generic LLM behavior). Then sort findings into two groups. Quality issues such as verbosity, layout and small errors are fixed with prompts and examples. Safety issues such as harmful instructions, leaked personal data or biased treatment need guardrails. Bias is a pattern across outputs, so test it with paired inputs that differ only in one attribute, such as a name. The bias test and these review habits are generic practice, not Databricks features.

concepts.heading: Automating the review with MLflow judges
concepts.body: Manual reading finds new failure types; judges then count them across a dataset. MLflow ships built-in LLM judges that run inside `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`. `RetrievalRelevance` asks whether the retrieved context is relevant to the request, `RetrievalGroundedness` asks whether the response is grounded in that context, `RelevanceToQuery` checks that the answer addresses the question, and `Safety` checks for harmful or toxic content. All four need only `inputs` and `outputs`, so no ground truth. `Correctness` compares the answer with `expectations`, so it does need ground truth. For rules that belong to your business, such as "never promises a refund" or "never shows internal ticket IDs", a `Guidelines` judge checks natural-language criteria and returns pass or fail. Write one testable statement per guideline so the results show which rule failed. Match the symptom to the judge: an unsupported claim is a groundedness failure, while irrelevant retrieved text is a retrieval-relevance failure. Judge scores are evidence that supports the trace reading, not a replacement for it.

concepts.heading: Choosing chunking from evaluation results
concepts.body: Databricks describes finding the proper chunking method as iterative and context dependent, with no one-size-fits-all approach: the best size and method depend on the use case and the data. Chunk size, overlap and metadata are the knobs to test (generic list). So the choice is made by measurement. Use one fixed set of realistic questions, change one variable per run (chunk size first, then overlap, then splitter), re-index each time and compare retrieval and answer metrics side by side. Read the pattern. Good recall at k with faithful but incomplete answers, where the missing details sit next to the retrieved chunk, means too little context, so larger chunks, overlap or parent-child expansion help. Falling precision at k after overlap was raised, with near-duplicate hits filling the top results, means too much overlap. A mixed corpus rarely has one best splitter: keep a short FAQ entry whole, split manuals on headings with `MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter`, and store a `doc_type` column so results can be evaluated by source. If small chunks win on lookups and large ones win on procedures, index small units and expand them with parent-child or sentence-window retrieval (both generic patterns).

examPoints: A scenario that names a Markdown, HTML, FAQ or mixed corpus asks you to match the splitter to the structure; a scenario that names an agent calling a governed SQL function asks for `UCFunctionToolkit` with the default serverless client, since local mode cannot run SQL functions.

A symptom story tells you where the fault is: irrelevant retrieved passages mean fix retrieval and measure `RetrievalRelevance`; an unsupported claim with correct passages means groundedness and the prompt; team-specific rules mean a `Guidelines` judge; `Correctness` is the judge that needs ground truth.

When a chunking comparison is described, the sound design keeps the question set fixed and changes one variable at a time; a single run, a changed embedding model plus a changed chunk size, or a gain of a few points on a tiny set are not evidence.

quiz.q: A RAG assistant tells a user that the premium plan includes 24/7 phone support. The retrieved passages in the MLflow trace mention only email support. Which diagnosis and automatic check fit?
choices: A retrieval miss, so the retrieved context should be scored for relevance before touching the model or the prompt wording at all
A groundedness failure, so score it with `RetrievalGroundedness` and restrict the prompt to the context
A truncation problem, so raise `max_tokens` and check the finish reason on every response
A safety failure, so add a `Safety` judge that blocks answers mentioning phone numbers
quiz.explain: The retrieved text does not contain the claim, so the model invented it: that is an ungrounded answer, which `RetrievalGroundedness` measures and a context-only prompt reduces. Relevance would be the check if the passages were off-topic, token limits cut answers short instead of adding claims, and the content is not harmful.

quiz.q: A knowledge base mixes 100-token FAQ entries with 40-page manuals that have chapter headings. One fixed 500-token splitter is used for everything, and a per-source evaluation shows diluted FAQ answers and manual answers cut across chunks. Which change fits?
choices: Raise the single chunk size to 2,000 tokens so that both kinds of source are covered by one setting
Switch to a smaller embedding model so that chunk boundaries become less important for the retriever
Add 60 percent overlap to the fixed splitter so neighboring entries share enough of their text
Split by source type: one chunk per FAQ entry, heading-based chunks for manuals, then re-evaluate
quiz.explain: The two sources have different structure, so one splitter cannot serve both. Whole-entry FAQ chunks and heading-based manual chunks follow the content, and the evaluation confirms the gain. A larger fixed size dilutes FAQs further, heavy overlap creates near-duplicate hits, and the embedding model does not decide chunk boundaries.

days.recap: Match the splitter to the format; `ChatDatabricks`, `VectorSearchRetrieverTool` and `UCFunctionToolkit` (serverless by default) are the Databricks LangChain pieces. Read traces to separate retrieval from generation faults, then use `RetrievalRelevance`, `RetrievalGroundedness`, `Safety` and `Guidelines` (no ground truth) versus `Correctness` (ground truth). Pick chunking from a fixed question set, one change per run.

days.title: Prompt Augmentation, Moving a Baseline Response and Guardrails

concepts.heading: Augmenting retrieval and prompts from the user's input
concepts.body: The user's own message carries three things worth mining: key fields (a product, a date range, an account id), key terms (an error code, an exact identifier) and intent (billing, technical, account). Key fields can be extracted with a small LLM call that returns JSON, or with rules, and then applied as metadata filters: a Databricks AI Search query accepts `filters` on indexed columns, so a question naming one pump model can search only that product's chunks. Key terms help the keyword half of hybrid search; with `query_type="hybrid"` AI Search merges similarity and keyword results using Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so an exact code still ranks well. Intent routes the request to the matching index, prompt or tool. A follow-up such as "and its battery life?" has no meaning for a retriever that sees one string, so condense the history and the new message into a standalone query first (generic pattern, one extra cheap call per turn). Trusted request fields such as language or account tier belong in template variables filled by the application, not guessed by the model.

concepts.heading: Structuring the prompt around the user text
concepts.body: When instructions, retrieved context and the user's question share one undivided block, the model can mistake parts of the question for instructions or lose track of where the evidence ends. A structured RAG prompt (generic practice) puts the instructions first: the role, the task and the rule to answer only from the supplied context. Then comes the context inside clear delimiters such as `<context>` tags, then the user's question in its own delimited section described as the question, and the required output format last. Add a fixed fallback reply for the missing-answer case, for example a short sentence saying the answer is not in the documents. Without that fallback the model fills the gap from memory. Delimiters and a stated fallback reduce confusion and ungrounded answers, but they ask the model to behave; they do not verify behavior. Anything that must never happen needs a check in the request path, which is the topic of the guardrail concept below. Test prompt changes against a fixed evaluation set rather than by feel.

concepts.heading: Moving a baseline response to the desired output
concepts.body: A baseline is whatever the first, simple prompt produces. Prompt engineering is a loop: read what is wrong with the baseline, change the prompt to close that one gap, measure again. The levers are generic. A specific instruction names the reader, the content to include, a size limit and a layout, so "Summarize this ticket" becomes "Summarize for a support agent in at most 60 words: the problem, the steps tried and the wanted outcome, as three labeled lines". Few-shot examples teach style, tone and layout better than description does: three to five approved question-and-reply pairs move a long, formal reply toward a short, friendly one. When one prompt carries several tasks and some are neglected, split it into chained prompts, one job each, and pass fields forward. Emphasis such as capital letters adds no information. Change one element per iteration and rerun the same fixed evaluation set; a five-element rewrite that raises a score from 70 to 74 percent teaches nothing about why. Log versions with their scores so the best one can be recovered.

concepts.heading: Guardrails: where they sit and what they do
concepts.body: A guardrail is a control in the request path that prevents a negative outcome and has a defined action when it fires (generic design, vendor neutral). On the input side, a cheap classifier or rule decides whether a request is in scope; for a bank assistant restricted to bank topics, return a fixed polite refusal, which also saves the main model call. On the output side, a safety classifier, rules or an LLM judge inspects the answer, and a failure returns a pre-written fallback or a regeneration. Functional guardrails fit RAG: a groundedness check against the retrieved passages, and validation of structured output against a schema with a retry. Logging and later review happen after the user has seen the content, so they are not guardrails. Streaming conflicts with output checks: either do not stream on the safety-critical path or buffer and check text before release. Shared baseline rules belong at one entry point in front of the model; Unity Gateway is documented as that governed layer for models, agents and MCP servers. AI Guardrails for serving endpoints is Public Preview, so rely on these principles.

examPoints: A question about using the user's words to improve retrieval expects extraction of key fields into metadata filters, key terms into the keyword part of a hybrid query, or intent into routing; a follow-up with pronouns expects a standalone rewritten query.

A baseline that varies in length or tone is fixed with a more specific instruction or few-shot examples; a prompt that neglects sub-tasks is fixed by chaining; an unexplained gain from changing many things at once calls for one change per run on the same evaluation set.

When unsafe or off-topic text must never reach users, pick a control in the request path (input classifier with refusal, output check with fallback); logging, monitoring and instructions in the system prompt alone are not guardrails, and a check that waits for a streamed answer to finish is too late.

quiz.q: A user asks, "What is the warranty on the X200 pump?" An AI Search index holds chunks for many products and has a `product` metadata column. Which step uses the user's input to narrow retrieval?
choices: Extract the product name from the question and use it as a metadata filter on the query
Embed the question twice and average the two vectors before searching the whole index of all products
Add every product name to the system prompt so the model chooses which chunks to read
Increase the number of results returned so that the right product is likely to appear
quiz.explain: A key field in the question (the product) becomes a filter on an indexed column, so only that product's chunks are searched. Averaging vectors, listing products in the prompt and returning more results leave the search space unchanged or add noise and cost.

quiz.q: A streaming chat application checks the full answer for unsafe content only after the model finishes, but users read tokens as they stream and unsafe text is already visible when the check blocks the answer. Which fix keeps the guardrail?
choices: Tell the model in the system prompt to avoid unsafe text, which makes the separate output check unnecessary
Log every blocked answer to a table so that a reviewer can examine it the next morning
Buffer and check chunks before they reach the interface, or skip streaming on the safety-critical path
Lower the temperature to zero so that the same unsafe text is never generated again
quiz.explain: A guardrail only helps if it runs before the user sees the text, so the check must precede release: buffer and check in pieces, or do not stream where safety matters. A prompt asks but does not verify, logging happens afterwards, and temperature does not guarantee safe output.

days.recap: Mine the question for key fields (metadata filters), key terms (hybrid keyword match) and intent (routing); rewrite follow-ups into standalone queries. Structure prompts with delimited context, an answer-only-from-context rule and a fallback. Improve a baseline by specificity, few-shot or chaining, one change per run. Guardrails are input or output checks with a defined action, placed before the user sees text.

days.title: Choosing the LLM, the Embedding Model and the Metrics

concepts.heading: Selecting an LLM from application attributes
concepts.body: There is no best model in general; match the attributes of the application to the attributes of the model (generic selection practice). Task difficulty decides quality needs: reasoning-heavy or open-ended work needs a stronger model, while a store-hours chat widget with one-sentence answers and high traffic is served by a small, fast, cheap one. Interactive use rewards low latency; volume makes cost per request matter. The context window is a hard requirement: if a 150,000-token contract plus instructions plus the answer exceeds it, the model is excluded before quality is even compared. On Databricks, hosted models are served as model services in `system.ai`, but seeing one there does not mean your workspace can call it: availability depends on workspace region, cross-geography routing for global endpoints and whether you hold query permission. Capacity is a separate choice: pay-per-token is the shared option, on-demand provisioned throughput gives dedicated capacity with no term commitment, and reserved provisioned throughput reserves dedicated capacity for a fixed 1- or 3-month term. Matching them to variable versus sustained traffic is generic reasoning.

concepts.heading: Embedding window, dimension and the context window
concepts.body: Three numbers are easy to confuse. The embedding window is the maximum input an embedding model reads for one text; longer text is truncated, so details in the cut part cannot be retrieved. The embedding dimension is the length of the output vector and must match the index definition. The chat model's context window is a separate limit on prompt plus answer. The Foundation Model APIs documentation lists two hosted text embedding models, both with 1,024-dimension vectors: GTE Large (En) with an 8,192-token embedding window and BGE Large (En) with 512. A 1,200-token chunk therefore fits GTE but is truncated by BGE. A bigger window is capacity, not quality: if every FAQ entry is about 120 tokens, a larger window changes nothing, and any gain must be measured with retrieval metrics. Then budget the chat prompt: instructions plus chunks times chunk size plus answer must fit the context window. With 500 instruction tokens, a 600-token answer and a 4,096-token window, 5 chunks of 1,500 tokens (7,500) fail, while 5 chunks of 500 tokens give 500 + 2,500 + 600 = 3,600 and fit. Documents and queries share one embedding model.

concepts.heading: Model hubs, Marketplace listings and model cards
concepts.body: Models can come from several places, and the metadata decides eligibility before any technical test. Databricks Marketplace lets you filter listings by product type (dataset or ML model), provider name, category and cost (free or paid). Some listings are free and instantly available after you accept terms; "By request" ones need provider approval. Whatever you obtain appears in your workspace as a read-only catalog in Unity Catalog, which needs at least the `USE MARKETPLACE ASSETS` privilege on the metastore. Because the shared catalog is read-only, any modified copy, such as a fine-tuned variant, has to be registered as a new model in a catalog you own (generic inference, not a Marketplace rule). A model card documents a model; for selection, read the intended use and limits, the training languages and evaluation results, the license and terms of use, and the size and format. A Korean-and-Japanese support bot needs a model trained and evaluated in those languages, and a paid customer-facing product needs a license that permits commercial use. Databricks states that you are responsible for complying with the applicable model terms wherever a model is hosted.

concepts.heading: Choosing a model from experiment metrics
concepts.body: MLflow tracking stores each run with parameters (model name, prompt version, temperature) and metrics (correctness, latency, tokens). Runs of one experiment can be compared side by side in the workspace, and the MLflow client `search_runs` returns a pandas DataFrame you can sort and filter in code. Log the same metrics for every candidate on the same evaluation questions, apply hard constraints such as latency, then take the best quality among the runs that qualify. Useful metrics discriminate between candidates: correctness or groundedness scores, plus latency and tokens per request. Metrics that do not help are parameter count, pretraining loss and generic leaderboard rank; a public benchmark builds a shortlist but does not replace a held-out set of your own questions. Treat small gaps with care: if two configurations swap places on rerun, the difference is noise, so enlarge the set before deciding (generic statistics). When a word-overlap score such as ROUGE favors one summarizer but reviewers prefer the other, add a semantic metric such as an LLM judge and check it against human preferences (generic evaluation practice: overlap metrics reward matching words, not meaning).

examPoints: A scenario with short, simple, high-volume questions points to a small fast model; a long-document scenario points first to the context window; a regulated-industry scenario where a listed model is rejected points to workspace region, cross-geo settings and query permission.

Chunk size is limited by the embedding window (truncation beyond it), the vector length is the embedding dimension, and retrieved text plus instructions plus answer is limited by the chat model's context window; recompute the budget and, when switching embedding models, re-embed the whole corpus.

A model-choice question that offers popularity, parameter count or a single benchmark rank loses to one that uses model-card languages and license plus the team's own evaluation questions, compared side by side in an MLflow experiment.

quiz.q: A team indexes procedures in chunks of about 1,200 tokens, and each procedure must stay in one chunk. They can pick a hosted embedding model with a 512-token embedding window or one with an 8,192-token embedding window, both producing 1,024-dimension vectors. Which should they choose and why?
choices: The 512-token model, because a smaller window forces the model to focus on the key sentences
Either one, because the dimension is equal and the dimension decides how much text is embedded, so the window size does not matter
The 8,192-token model, because the whole 1,200-token chunk then fits into the embedding window
The 512-token model, because the chat model then receives smaller chunks in its prompt
quiz.explain: Text beyond the embedding window is truncated, so a 1,200-token chunk loses more than half its content with a 512-token window. The dimension only sets the vector length, and the chat prompt size is governed by the chat model's context window, not the embedding window.

quiz.q: A data scientist logs five prompt-and-model configurations as MLflow runs with correctness, latency and token metrics on the same evaluation questions. What is the simplest sound way to choose among them?
choices: Pick the run with the largest model, since model size predicts quality on any task and any data set at all
Compare the runs side by side in the experiment, apply the latency limit, then pick the best quality
Choose the run that was logged most recently, since the last attempt reflects the best prompt
Take the model that ranks first on a public leaderboard and ignore the logged results
quiz.explain: Runs hold the parameters and metrics needed for a controlled comparison on the same data; applying the constraints first and then maximizing quality gives a reproducible choice. Size, recency and leaderboard rank do not measure this application.

days.recap: Match model to task difficulty, latency, cost, context window, inputs and languages; `system.ai` listing is not availability. Embedding window truncates, dimension is vector length, context window limits prompt plus answer. Marketplace listings are filtered by type, provider and cost and arrive as read-only catalogs; read model cards for languages and license. Compare MLflow runs on the same questions.

days.title: Agent Framework, Evaluation versus Monitoring and the Genie API

concepts.heading: Authoring agents with ResponsesAgent
concepts.body: Databricks recommends the MLflow interface `ResponsesAgent` for production agents. It is framework neutral: build the agent with LangGraph, the OpenAI SDK, DSPy or plain Python, and `ResponsesAgent` connects it to Databricks logging, tracing, evaluation and deployment. Its schema is compatible with the OpenAI Responses schema; the older `ChatAgent` is not recommended for new agents. An existing LangGraph agent is not rewritten: write a class that inherits from `mlflow.pyfunc.ResponsesAgent`, keep the agent as an attribute, implement `predict` to convert the request messages into the agent's format and the output back into a `ResponsesAgentResponse`, and add `predict_stream` for streaming. Documented benefits are multi-message output including intermediate tool calls, streaming, automatic signature inference when you log the agent, and automatic tracing of `predict` and `predict_stream`. For streaming, emit several `output_text.delta` events sharing one `item_id`, then a final `response.output_item.done` event with the same `item_id` and the full text; without the done event the trace and the aggregated inference record never receive a complete answer.

concepts.heading: Logging, resources and deploying with Agent Framework
concepts.body: An agent is logged with MLflow, registered to Unity Catalog and deployed with `agents.deploy(uc_model_name, version)` from `databricks.agents`, which creates a Model Serving endpoint, provisions authentication for the resources the agent declared, enables MLflow tracing and sets up the Review App. Databricks-managed resources such as an AI Search index, a Unity Catalog function or a Genie Agent are declared in the `resources` argument when logging; for a Genie Agent the class is `DatabricksGenieSpace`. At deployment Databricks verifies that the endpoint creator can access every declared dependency, creates a service principal for the model version and injects short-lived credentials that it rotates. A notebook-tested agent that gets permission errors on the endpoint usually never declared the resource: declare it, give the creator the needed permission (`CAN RUN` for a Genie Agent) and redeploy. Calling `deploy()` again with the same model name adds the new version to the existing endpoint, and the old version keeps serving until traffic shifts, so changing only the version gives a zero-downtime update. For new agents the docs now recommend the Agent Bricks CLI and Databricks Apps, though Model Serving deployment remains documented.

concepts.heading: Evaluation phase versus monitoring phase
concepts.body: Agent quality is a loop, and the two phases differ in what they run on. Evaluation happens before release: you run scorers (LLM judges and code checks) over a fixed, curated evaluation dataset with `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` and compare app versions on the same inputs, so any difference comes from the change and not from different traffic. A dataset with reference answers also allows ground-truth judges such as `Correctness`. Choosing between two prompt versions before launch is therefore an evaluation task. Monitoring happens after release: the same scorers run on a sample of real production traces, which reveals drift such as users asking about a new product line the dataset never covered. Sampling trades coverage against judge cost. Databricks documents production monitoring of agents as Beta, so treat it as the concept of scoring live traces, not as a settled product answer. The loop closes when failing production traces become new evaluation records and the fixed agent is re-evaluated against the old version. Request logs are deprecated in favor of MLflow 3 tracing.

concepts.heading: The Genie Agents conversational API
concepts.body: Genie Agents (formerly Genie spaces) answer data questions in natural language over governed tables, and the Genie Agents API lets your own application or agent use them. It has three groups. Chat mode APIs hold stateful conversations, so a follow-up such as "Now only for EMEA" uses the earlier history, and you can retrieve the generated SQL, results and visualizations. Agent mode APIs send prompts in Agent mode, stream the reasoning and SQL results and return a final report with citations. Management APIs create, configure and deploy Genie Agents across workspaces for CI/CD. Sending prompts needs at least CAN VIEW on the agent and `SELECT` on the data, and data access is evaluated with the caller's own Unity Catalog permissions. Messages are processed asynchronously, so the client polls the status every 1 to 5 seconds, increasing the delay with exponential backoff up to one minute, until `COMPLETED`, `FAILED` or `CANCELLED`, and stops with a timeout after 10 minutes. The API does not retry failed requests, so add your own retries. Start a new conversation for each session.

examPoints: A scenario with an existing LangGraph or LangChain agent that needs tracing, an inferred signature and Playground or evaluation compatibility is solved by wrapping it in a `ResponsesAgent` subclass, not by rewriting it; streamed answers that never show a complete trace need one shared `item_id` and a closing `response.output_item.done` event.

Choosing between two versions before release, on a curated dataset, is evaluation with `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`; catching quality drops from new real-world questions is monitoring of production traces; failing traces are turned into evaluation records, and the fix is re-evaluated.

For Genie in an agent: follow-ups need Chat mode (stateful), deep investigations with cited reports need Agent mode, multi-workspace CI/CD needs the Management APIs, long answers need polling with backoff, and a deployed endpoint that cannot call Genie needs the resource declared at logging plus `CAN RUN` for the endpoint creator.

quiz.q: A registered agent already runs on a Model Serving endpoint created by `agents.deploy()`. The team registers a new version and calls `agents.deploy()` again with the same Unity Catalog model name and no other changes. What happens?
choices: A second endpoint with a new name is created, and every client must be switched over to it by hand
The existing endpoint is deleted first, so requests fail for a while until the new version has fully started and passed its health checks
The call is rejected because a deployment for that model name already exists on that endpoint
The new version joins the existing endpoint and takes traffic once ready; the old one keeps serving
quiz.explain: With the same model name, deploy adds the new version to the existing endpoint; the previous version serves until the shift, so in-flight requests are not interrupted. Changing only the version is what keeps the update zero-downtime.

quiz.q: A supervisor agent calls a Genie Agent as a tool. A user asks "Revenue by region for last quarter?" and then "Now only for EMEA." The second question must use the first as context. How should the integration call the API?
choices: Use the Chat mode APIs, which keep a stateful conversation so follow-ups use the earlier history
Use the Management APIs, which create a fresh Genie Agent for every question in the dialogue
Open a new conversation for each question and paste the earlier SQL into the later message by hand
Use the Agent mode APIs, since a final cited report is always required before a follow-up works
quiz.explain: Chat mode conversations are stateful, so the follow-up is resolved against the earlier question. Management APIs configure agents rather than answer questions, a new conversation per question loses history, and Agent mode is for streamed investigations with reports.

days.recap: Wrap existing agents in `ResponsesAgent` (`predict`, `predict_stream`, shared `item_id` plus a done event). `agents.deploy()` builds the endpoint, tracing and Review App; declare managed resources at logging, same-name redeploy is zero-downtime. Evaluation compares versions on a fixed dataset; monitoring scores live traces. Genie API: Chat mode for follow-ups, Agent mode for cited reports, Management for CI/CD, poll with backoff.

days.title: Packaging Chains as pyfunc Models and Securing Endpoint Access

concepts.heading: Custom pyfunc for pre- and post-processing
concepts.body: When a chain needs more than one model call, wrap it in a custom Python function model. Databricks lists the reasons: the model needs preprocessing before its predict function, the framework is not natively supported by MLflow, the raw output must be post-processed for the consumer, the model has per-request branching logic, or you deploy fully custom code. You subclass `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel` and write two functions. `load_context` holds anything loaded once, such as weights or a tokenizer, so inference stays fast. `predict` holds everything that runs on every request: clean the input, call the model, turn logits into a label and a confidence string. Logging the class produces one artifact and one endpoint that contains the whole chain, so clients do not repeat cleaning or formatting code. One packaging detail: Databricks Runtime ML ships `mlflow-skinny`, but Model Serving needs `mlflow`, so name `mlflow` in `pip_requirements` when you log. A natively supported flavor with no extra logic does not need the wrapper.

concepts.heading: Files and parameters that travel with the model
concepts.body: A serving endpoint runs in its own container, so the notebook's disk and your volume paths are not there. Model Serving requires files from Unity Catalog volumes to be packaged into the model artifact: pass the `artifacts` dictionary to `log_model`, mapping a name to a path, and read the path from `context.artifacts` inside `load_context`. Shared helper modules travel with `code_path`. Real-time workloads perform best when dependencies are captured at logging time, so downloading files at startup is the pattern to avoid. Values that change between environments, such as the chat endpoint name, retriever settings or prompt text, belong in `ModelConfig`: key-value parameters taken from a Python dictionary during development or from a `.yaml` file for production and CI/CD. The agent code reads them with `model_config.get(...)`, and you pass the `model_config` parameter to `log_model` so the logged agent loads that set. The code file stays identical in development, staging and production, and the logged model records the parameters it was built with.

concepts.heading: Controlling access to and from serving endpoints
concepts.body: Two directions matter. Who may call the endpoint is set by its ACL: CAN VIEW gets and lists it, CAN QUERY adds querying, and CAN MANAGE adds updating the configuration, deleting it and changing permissions. An app or service principal that only sends requests gets CAN QUERY. What the deployed chain may reach is set by authentication. Automatic authentication passthrough is the recommended method when every resource supports it. You declare resources (AI Search index, Unity Catalog function, chat model endpoint, SQL warehouse, Genie Agent) when logging. At deployment Databricks verifies that the endpoint creator can use each one, creates a service principal for the model version, grants it access and injects short-lived credentials that it rotates. So the creator needs, for example, `Can Use` on an index, `EXECUTE` on a function, `Can Query` on an endpoint, `Can Run` on a Genie Agent or `Use Endpoint` on a warehouse, plus `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` on the parents of Unity Catalog resources. Manual authentication means long-lived credentials you rotate yourself.

concepts.heading: Simple chains (generic LangChain pattern)
concepts.body: This part is generic LangChain expression language (LCEL) behavior, not a Databricks feature. A chain is a fixed sequence chosen by the developer: retriever, prompt template, chat model, output parser, written `retriever | prompt | model | parser`. Each component consumes the previous output, and the first component defines the input contract. A template with `{context}` and `{question}` needs a mapping with exactly those keys, so a request that sends `query` fails while the prompt renders, before the model is called. Repair it with a mapping step in front of the prompt, for example a dictionary of runnables that fills `context` from the retriever and `question` from the incoming field. The last step is an output parser: to return JSON the prompt states the keys and the parser validates them. Use a chain when the path never depends on a model decision, such as a fixed lookup followed by an answer. An agent lets the model choose tools, which adds model calls, variance and evaluation effort.

examPoints: A question about cleaning input, turning logits into a label, per-request branching or an unsupported framework behind one endpoint is testing a custom `pyfunc` model with `load_context` and `predict`.

A question about weights or templates that must exist on the endpoint, or about changing only the endpoint name or prompt between environments, is testing `artifacts` with `context.artifacts` or `ModelConfig` passed as `model_config`.

A question about who may query an endpoint points to CAN QUERY; a question about deployment failing for the creator or about short-lived rotated credentials points to resources declared at logging and automatic authentication passthrough.

quiz.q: A text classifier needs cleaned, tokenized input and must return a label with a confidence string instead of raw logits, all behind one endpoint. Its weights and a tokenizer folder sit in a Unity Catalog volume. How should the team package it?
choices: Log the raw model alone, put the cleaning and formatting code in every client application, and point those clients at the one endpoint
Subclass `PythonModel`, pass volume paths in `artifacts`, load them in `load_context`, and clean and format in `predict`
Keep the cleaning code in a Git repository and let the endpoint clone it and read the volume paths when the first request arrives
Log the raw model with a native flavor and mount the volume on the serving container so a script reformats each response afterwards
quiz.explain: One custom pyfunc model with `load_context` and `predict` gives a single self-contained endpoint, and `artifacts` packages the volume files into the model. Client-side logic drifts, runtime cloning adds a dependency the logged model does not capture, and a mounted volume is not part of the artifact.

quiz.q: A RAG agent is logged with an AI Search index and a Unity Catalog function declared as resources, then deployed with automatic authentication passthrough. Deployment fails for the data scientist who ran it. What explains the failure?
choices: The endpoint's own service principal lacks CAN MANAGE on the serving endpoint that Databricks created for the agent model version, so it cannot start
Passthrough cannot be combined with a Unity Catalog function, so the function must be called with a personal access token instead of declared resources
The agent must be deployed with manual authentication first, because passthrough only works after long-lived credentials exist
Databricks checks that the deployer can use each declared resource, and she lacks `EXECUTE` on the function or its parent usage rights
quiz.explain: With passthrough, Databricks first verifies that the endpoint creator can access each declared resource, then grants a created service principal access. A missing `EXECUTE`, `USE SCHEMA` or `USE CATALOG` for the creator blocks the deployment; the other statements invent requirements.

days.recap: Package multi-step chains as a custom pyfunc (`load_context` once, `predict` per request), ship files with `artifacts` and vary prompt or endpoint with `ModelConfig`. CAN QUERY is the least privilege for callers. Declare resources at logging so passthrough gives short-lived credentials, provided the creator can use them. Chains are fixed paths (generic LCEL); agents let the model choose.

days.title: Logging RAG Chains, Registering Them and Building AI Search Indexes

concepts.heading: Basic elements of a RAG application
concepts.body: A RAG application has a handful of parts to decide before logging: the model flavor, the chat model and embedding model it calls, the retriever, the package dependencies, an input example and a signature. Databricks recommends code-based logging (Models from Code): the chain or agent is a Python file that ends with `mlflow.models.set_model(chain)`, and `mlflow.langchain.log_model(lc_model="agent.py", ...)` stores that file. When the model is loaded or served, the file runs again to rebuild the chain, and a request calls `invoke`. Custom code takes the same route through `mlflow.pyfunc.log_model`. Pass `resources` so passthrough credentials can be provisioned for the index and endpoints. The signature, the input and output schema, lets AI Playground and the review app call the agent. For a `ResponsesAgent`, the interface Databricks recommends, MLflow infers a valid signature and you can skip the step. For a LangChain chain or generic pyfunc code you define a signature or pass an `input_example`, which must be a valid input to the model, and MLflow infers the signature from it.

concepts.heading: Registering in Unity Catalog and deploying
concepts.body: Registration puts the logged artifact under Unity Catalog governance.
